We discussed that a bit. Before this PR, `force_update` used to do two things: 1) notify _runtime_tile_data* methods might lead to different results and 2) trigger a direct update instead of waiting till the end of the frame.

Initially, I made `force_update` only do 2), and created `notify_runtime_tile_data_update` to cover 1). This is a cleanup and a bit of a optimization, as notifying several times would not trigger several unneeded updates. The naming was likely the most expected according to what each of those new function do. 

However, the main issue is that `force_update()` seemed mostly used for 2). This means that, in most cases, this would break users' code without them knowing what's wrong or triggering any error. That's was we decided to create an `update_now` function instead, and deprecate `force_update`. That would allow users to keep their code working.

But the current `update_now` function is a bit unrelated. Basically all TileMap update (like, physics, rendering, navigation, scenes, etc...) are pushed to the end of the frame. This makes it so all TileMap internals (bodies, canvas items, child scenes, etc...) are not accessible right after a property change on the TileMap. 

For example, if you paint a scene tile, the actual scene will be added only at the end of the frame. That's where you might want to call `update_now` right away, so that you could access some internal data earlier on:
```gdscript
$TileMap.set_cell(0, position, 0, Vector2i(0,0)) # Set a scene tile.
$TileMap.get_child_count() # returns 0

$TileMap.update_now()
$TileMap.get_child_count() # returns 1
```

issue_context.title: PathFollower2D Does NOT Update the Position and Collision of Child Tilemap with collision_animatable True
issue_context.body:
### Godot version

4.1.x

### System information

Windows 11

### Issue description

When a Tilemap node is attached as a child node of PathFollower2D node, with `collision_animatable` on in the inspector, the tilemap will stuck at (0, 0) if you scripted the movement of the PathFollower2D node with `progress` changed; while the tiles run as usual if `collision_animatable` is **false**.
This is very weird because the documentation said that "you can make Animatablebody2D move with script", and I used but it feedbacked a strange result, which is unacceptable and unwilling to see.
More detailed info please see the minimal project

P.S. Only under PathFollower2D, you add a RemoteTransformer2D that linked to a Tilemap can the tiles move as usual with `collision_animatable` on.

### Steps to reproduce

In the minimal reproduction project:

1. Make the `collision_animatable` of Tilemap and run the project, and you can see the tilemap moves as usual
2. Then tick on the property and run the game again, in which you can see the tilemap stuck at (0, 0) permanently.

### Minimal reproduction project

[bug report.zip](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/files/12094949/bug.report.zip)

review_comments: If it's debug then it should be all wrapped in `#ifdef DEBUG_ENABLED` I think. Only parts of the debug update are conditional...
I don't know. From what I could read, it seems like it is not done for drawing collision shape in general. So, I am not sure we can add a condition here.

Collision shapes can only draw in debug build.
What I mean is that the debug code should not run at all in release builds. Meantime the `_debug_update()` is always called and wastes performance when not needed.

> Collision shapes can only draw in debug build.

If that's the case, then yes, I can wrap the code in `#ifdef DEBUG_ENABLED` then. I'll do that.
Would it be significantly slower to collect items to delete and then do the clearing? This feels very error prone.
The same "hack" is used for SceneTreeTimers and Tweens.

Well my question is if it's used for a good reason or because it was just simpler to write code this way 🙃 There is no natural increment in the loop's definition, so a tiny mistake can make it go on forever. Same applies to any other place that uses this trick.

The problem is that the whole point of SelfList is to limit allocations to a minimum. If I allocate a structure to list the objects to delete, there's little gain into using a SelfList at all. 

I believe (didn't test) the performance gain likely depends on how many quadrants you have, but I guess it could get quite big with Y-sorting enabled, as the quadrant size is reduced to 1 tile = 1 quadrant.

In any case, I called that a "hack" as, like, it's a bit of a weird implementation. But TBH, I think it's perfectly fine. There's no reason the pointer should point to garbage, even if the SelfList implementation changed, as we are basically pointing an object that is allocated by the TileMap. I could remove the comment if that's a bit bothering.

I'm not bothered by the comment. In fact, if the code remains as is, I'd prefer the comment to remain as well. The danger comes from the fact that there is no increment/iteration statement in the for-loop definition. So it can be easy to make a mistake and end up with an endless loop. It's just a code style issue that I'm pointing at, and the question about performance was just me wondering if the sacrifice in code clarity/stability is worth it because of a bigger gain somewhere else.

Are that many flags actually needed? Some of them seem unused or have duplicate usage.

Also you are using them with a bool array, but the assigned value resets in the middle (`DIRTY_FLAGS_TILE_MAP_IN_TREE `). This doesn't seem right.

This is a `struct`, so it's already public.
Not sure why didn't you use `class` though.
Should probably be wrapped too, as the class is unused in release.
